lesson.title: Susan B. Anthony: The Organizer Who Built the Movement's Machinery
lesson.summary: Susan B. Anthony turned women's rights from a scattered set of grievances into a disciplined political movement, even standing trial in 1873 for the act of casting a vote.
lesson.body:
Susan B. Anthony was born on February 15, 1820, in Adams, Massachusetts, into a Quaker family that valued education and social reform. That upbringing pushed her first toward the temperance and abolitionist movements, where she learned the practical skills of organizing petitions, running meetings, and building coalitions. She soon found that women were often barred from speaking or holding leadership roles even within reform movements they had helped build, and that experience convinced her that women needed direct political power of their own, not just a voice within other people's causes.

In 1851 Anthony met Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and the two formed a partnership that would drive the fight for women's rights for decades. Stanton was the movement's most gifted writer and theorist, while Anthony proved to be its tireless organizer, traveling constantly, building networks of local activists, and keeping the cause funded and visible. Together they founded the National Woman Suffrage Association in 1869, an organization that pushed for a federal constitutional amendment rather than relying only on state-by-state campaigns.

Anthony's commitment to the cause became a matter of public record in a very literal way. In November 1872 she voted in the presidential election in Rochester, New York, deliberately testing the argument that the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantee of citizenship rights already implied a right to vote for women. She was arrested, tried, and in 1873 convicted and fined one hundred dollars, a fine she refused to pay for the rest of her life. The trial became a piece of movement theater, generating publicity and sympathy even in defeat. Anthony died on March 13, 1906, fourteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment she had spent her life pursuing was finally ratified, but the organizational structure and legal arguments she built became the foundation for the broader women's suffrage movement that carried the fight to its conclusion.
